speaker: ALEX
text: Episode 0 sets the map: what this workshop is, how the two days fit together, and what you will be able to do by the end. I want the path to feel clear, teachable, and recoverable when the screen changes.

speaker: JAMIE
text: And I can be the learner voice here: what is this for, where am I, and how do I know I did it right?

speaker: ALEX
text: The headline is simple. You are stepping into open source, and that matters because open source is shared work: code, issues, reviews, and improvements that people can see, discuss, and build on together. In GitHub terms, a repository is the project home, an issue is a tracked task or question, a pull request is a proposed change, and a merge is what brings that change into the main line.

speaker: JAMIE
text: So this episode is the tour before the first real rep.

speaker: ALEX
text: Exactly. We name the idea, show why it matters, then point to the checks that tell you you are on track.

speaker: JAMIE
text: How should someone picture the workshop itself?

speaker: ALEX
text: Think of it as GitHub Learning Room, your complete workshop companion. It is the table of contents, the guidebook, and the reference shelf for the whole experience. The live agenda is only part of it; the self-paced curriculum carries the rest.

speaker: ALEX
text: That means the course works in two modes at once. Live sessions focus on the core path so everyone can make progress together. The full chapters, appendices, and exercises stay available for preparation, catch-up, remote participation, and follow-up after the event.

speaker: JAMIE
text: So the workshop is not just a class session. It is a path you can return to.

speaker: ALEX
text: Right. The goal is not speed. The goal is knowing what happened, what changed, and what to do next.

speaker: ALEX
text: Here is the two-day shape. Day 1 is GitHub Foundations in the browser. Day 2 moves to VS Code and accessibility agents on the desktop.

speaker: JAMIE
text: What does Day 1 actually cover?

speaker: ALEX
text: Day 1 is where you learn the web workflow with keyboard and screen reader support: finding a repository, opening issues, working with branches, making commits, and creating your first pull request. It is the browser-first day because you are learning the human process before the tooling gets more automated.

speaker: JAMIE
text: And Day 2?

speaker: ALEX
text: Day 2 is where the same habits shift into VS Code, GitHub Copilot, local Git, and the Accessibility Agents ecosystem. The workshop includes 55 accessibility agents across 3 teams, and they help with scanning, diagnosing, and remediating accessibility issues so the contribution work can scale.

speaker: ALEX
text: That is the learning arc too. First you do the manual version by hand. Then you see how automation supports the same workflow. If you understand the task yourself, the agent output becomes useful instead of mysterious.

speaker: JAMIE
text: So the lesson is not "trust the tool." It is "understand the move first."

speaker: ALEX
text: Exactly. Learn the manual skill first, then let automation accelerate it.

speaker: JAMIE
text: What should a beginner know before starting?

speaker: ALEX
text: Before you begin, make sure you have the basics in place: a GitHub account, Git installed if the course asks for it, VS Code ready for Day 2, and a screen reader configured if you use one. If you are new to the command line or Git, that is okay. The workshop is built to introduce the pieces gently and repeat the important patterns.

speaker: ALEX
text: The companion audio series helps too. Each episode mirrors a course topic in a short, teachable format, so you can listen while commuting, walking, or taking a break from the screen. It is there when audio helps you understand or revisit a step.

speaker: JAMIE
text: That makes the course feel less like a wall of instructions and more like a system.

speaker: ALEX
text: That is the point. Confidence comes from having a way back.

speaker: ALEX
text: The chapters are arranged to be read and practiced in order. Day 1 walks you through GitHub Foundations. Day 2 moves into VS Code and accessibility agents. The appendices sit beside the main path as reference material, not homework.

speaker: JAMIE
text: What belongs in those appendices?

speaker: ALEX
text: A few layers. Always open: the bookmarks you will use constantly. Core reference: the essentials you return to most often. Git deep dive: the deeper Git concepts. VS Code and Copilot: the desktop workflow and AI support. GitHub platform: the broader service and collaboration pieces. Community and continuing: where to go next after the workshop.

speaker: JAMIE
text: So the appendices are a side shelf, not a side quest.

speaker: ALEX
text: Exactly. Use them when you need them.

speaker: ALEX
text: Exercises are lightweight on purpose. The pattern repeats: Try It, You are done when, What success feels like. That gives you a short move, a clear finish line, and a human description of what good feels like.

speaker: JAMIE
text: That sounds much kinder than "complete the task."

speaker: ALEX
text: It is kinder, and it is clearer.

speaker: JAMIE
text: What should someone do when they get stuck?

speaker: ALEX
text: Use the support built into the course. Read the latest bot feedback, check the challenge issue, and ask for help with the page link and the place where you stopped. If the course points you to a support issue, use it. If the screen changed, describe what you saw and what you expected. Naming the exact control or page usually gets you unstuck faster.

speaker: JAMIE
text: That is especially helpful if you are navigating with a screen reader.

speaker: ALEX
text: Yes. The named thing is the handhold.

speaker: ALEX
text: That is why the workshop at a glance matters too. Start with your starting place, then accept the GitHub Classroom assignment, then open the Learning Room, then find Challenge 1, then choose the tool that fits the moment, listen for structure with a screen reader, use the built-in support, and check your first success before moving on.

speaker: JAMIE
text: So the first victory is not mastery. It is knowing where you are.

speaker: ALEX
text: Exactly.

speaker: ALEX
text: For sources, the guide points you back to authoritative references: GitHub Docs, GitHub Changelog, GitHub flow, About pull requests, About Git, GitHub Copilot docs, and the custom agents support matrix. The section-level source map tells you which references support which chapter, so when tools or pages change, you can verify the current behavior instead of guessing.

speaker: JAMIE
text: That matters because interfaces do change.

speaker: ALEX
text: They do. That is normal. The course is designed so you can recover by checking headings, landmarks, tab names, button labels, and the current URL instead of relying on memory alone.

speaker: JAMIE
text: What is the first real step?

speaker: ALEX
text: Know your starting place. Before Day 1, complete the setup chapter that helps you create or verify your account, confirm accessibility settings, install what you need, and get your screen reader and browser ready. If you stop there to check, you are not behind. You are building a clean entry point.

speaker: JAMIE
text: And the assignment comes after that?

speaker: ALEX
text: Yes. At the start of Day 1, accept the GitHub Classroom assignment. Open the link while signed in, authorize GitHub Classroom if asked, select your name if a roster appears, then accept the assignment. GitHub creates your private Learning Room repository from a template.

speaker: ALEX
text: From there, you refresh until the repository appears, open it, and bookmark it. You now have your own issues, branches, commits, and pull requests. That repository is your workspace, not a shared classroom board.

speaker: JAMIE
text: That helps the process feel concrete.

speaker: ALEX
text: Good. Concrete is what we want.

speaker: ALEX
text: Then you find the Learning Room and the first challenge. Challenge 1 tells you exactly where to start, what to read, and what evidence to post. The point is not to guess. The point is to follow the issue, complete the requested action, and close the loop when the instructions say you are done.

speaker: JAMIE
text: And if the page differs from the instructions?

speaker: ALEX
text: Check the current URL, the page title, the headings, and the tabs. If the label or order has shifted, re-orient before you act. That is the habit this course wants to build.

speaker: ALEX
text: Use the tool that fits the moment. GitHub.com in the browser is best for Day 1 and for repository navigation, issues, and pull requests. github.dev gives you a VS Code-style editor in the browser. VS Code desktop is the Day 2 home for local Git, Copilot, extensions, and deeper editing. GitHub Desktop is there if you want a visual Git client without typing commands.

speaker: JAMIE
text: So there is more than one right path.

speaker: ALEX
text: Yes. The course teaches the workflow first, then shows the different tools that can carry it.

speaker: ALEX
text: If you are listening with a screen reader, listen for structure before you move. Page title, repository name, landmarks like main content or navigation, and tab names like Code, Issues, or Pull requests tell you where you are. That is often enough to decide the next move safely.

speaker: JAMIE
text: That sounds like the difference between wandering and navigating.

speaker: ALEX
text: It is. Checkpoints turn uncertainty into information.

speaker: ALEX
text: When you need help, do not start over silently. Read the bot message, inspect the challenge issue, and ask for help with the exact page and step. The course also gives you reference solutions and chapter notes so you can compare what you did with what was expected.

speaker: JAMIE
text: That makes recovery part of the design.

speaker: ALEX
text: It is part of the design.

speaker: ALEX
text: Your first success check is simple. You can open your Learning Room repository. You can find the Issues tab. You can open Challenge 1. You know where to put your evidence and where to ask for help.

speaker: JAMIE
text: That is enough to keep going.

speaker: ALEX
text: It is more than enough.

speaker: ALEX
text: Where to go next is equally straightforward. Start with the setup chapter, then the tools chapter, then the GitHub basics, then repository navigation. After that, move into the Learning Room chapter and your first challenge. Keep the path explicit and the next step visible.

speaker: JAMIE
text: So the course keeps handing you the next rung.

speaker: ALEX
text: Exactly. That is the shape of the whole workshop.

speaker: ALEX
text: If you remember only one thing, remember this: know where you are, know what action you are taking, and know what confirmation should follow. If the confirmation is missing, pause and check. That is how the workflow becomes teachable instead of overwhelming.

speaker: JAMIE
text: And if someone is nervous about Git or the command line?

speaker: ALEX
text: Then the message is simple: you do not need to know everything before you begin. The workshop is built to help you learn by doing, with enough support to recover when you get lost.

speaker: ALEX
text: That is episode 0. Next, we move into the first chapter and start building the contributor muscle for real.
